title: Your client wants AI. How do you scope the implementation?
description: A guide for implementation firms turning a client's AI request into a workable scope, with clear deliverables, responsibilities and room for the larger operation to develop.
answer: A client can know what hurts before they know what needs to be built. They ask for an agent, a chatbot or an integration because those are the pieces they can name. Good Remedy works with the client and implementation firm to form the operation behind that request: the job, the people, the existing systems, the decisions and what has to happen when circumstances change. Then we agree on a complete first part to build.

sections.heading: The request is a starting point
paragraphs: Consider a client asking for an AI assistant to answer customer questions. The assistant needs information. But the service team also needs to know when an answer creates a commitment, who can change that commitment, and what delivery must receive. Connecting the assistant to documents will not settle those questions. The client may be describing a service operation through its most visible component.

Showing that wider operation gives the client a choice. Keep the first build narrow if that is what the business needs. Make its connections visible so the second build does not require undoing the first. A larger view should help control scope, not become an excuse to sell everything.

sections.heading: When the client asks for one piece
paragraphs: A client asks for an agent to review incoming requests. Building the review is only part of the job. Someone must establish which requests belong in the queue, what information the agent may use, what counts as a complete request, and where an uncertain result goes. The work also needs an owner after the implementation team hands it over.
These questions can change the scope of the build. Resolving them early gives the client and implementation firm something concrete to agree on, including what the first release will leave for later.

sections.heading: Follow the work through the people
paragraphs: Leadership may describe a growth goal. A department head translates it into a plan. An associate works through the actual queue, exceptions and customer conversations. The implementation has to connect those levels. A strategy that never reaches the work and an automation that cannot account for the strategy are both incomplete.

For the builder, that means agreeing on more than a successful API call. What does the next person receive? Can they tell what was decided? What happens if the request changes after that decision? Those answers belong in the build and its acceptance checks.

sections.heading: What the shared work produces
items: A map of the operation from incoming request to completed outcome.
An inventory of existing applications, records and AI tools, with a decision about what to keep or connect.
A buildable agreement covering inputs, outputs, responsibilities, exceptions and acceptance criteria.
An implementation plan with a coherent first release and an explicit path to the wider operation.
A handoff showing how the operation will be supported and changed after launch.

sections.heading: How the responsibilities can fit
paragraphs: Good Remedy can help form the work, define the operating architecture and participate in the agreed build. The implementation firm can contribute its client relationship, delivery team and platform specialization. The client retains the decisions that belong to its business. The actual division of implementation, support and commercial responsibilities is agreed for the engagement.

For example, a CRM implementation firm might build the integration while GR works with the client on what an approved account means, which exceptions need a person and what the delivery team must inherit from sales. This is an illustrative arrangement, not a report of a completed customer engagement.

sections.heading: A useful first conversation
paragraphs: Bring the client request, a description of the current process and the systems already involved. Identify where the team is confident and where it is still guessing. A useful outcome is an agreed next piece of work, its owner and the evidence needed to judge it.

questions: Do we have to replace our implementation team?
No. The engagement can be designed around the firm's existing team and technical strengths. Responsibilities and access should be agreed before work begins.
Is this just a requirements document?
The work should result in an operation that can be built, tested and used. Documentation supports that outcome; implementation responsibilities and deliverables belong in the agreed scope.
Can we start with one client function?
Yes. Start with a function that has a clear beginning, outcome and owner. Define how it connects to the rest of the client's work.

title: Who can help connect the AI tools we already bought?
description: A practical approach to connecting existing AI tools, CRM records, people and decisions across a business operation without starting from scratch.
answer: Start by deciding what the business needs to accomplish across its people and systems. Then decide what should connect. The tools and AI workspaces you already own are part of the starting material. Good Remedy helps form a shared operating structure around them, with a clear first implementation and a path for the connected operation to develop. Each integration still needs an access and feasibility check.

sections.heading: Your people may already be the integration
paragraphs: Someone reads a CRM record, checks a spreadsheet, asks a colleague what was agreed, pastes the answer into an AI chat and carries the result to the next team. The applications may all be functioning. The connection between them is being supplied by a person who remembers the job.

Before automating that work, make the decisions inside it visible. Which record wins when two disagree? Is the colleague explaining a fact or granting an exception? Does the next team need a summary, an approved instruction or a completed action? Passing the same text between applications does not preserve those differences by itself.

sections.heading: Follow one job all the way through
paragraphs: Consider a new customer moving from sales to onboarding to service delivery. Sales may have an AI research tool, onboarding may use a document assistant and delivery may have a project system. The business still needs the agreed scope, promises, approvals and unresolved questions to travel with the customer.

A useful operating design makes those shared facts explicit. It establishes where the current record lives, which system may update it and what happens when two records disagree. This example illustrates the design problem; it is not a customer result.

sections.heading: What to inventory
items: The actual steps people perform, including spreadsheets and manual work between applications.
Existing agents, prompts, integrations, AI workspaces and software subscriptions.
Records of customer commitments, current status and completed decisions.
People responsible for exceptions, approvals and ongoing support.
Access restrictions and the information that should stay in each existing system.

sections.heading: What an initial implementation can contain
paragraphs: A first release might connect intake, research, a human review queue and an approved handoff. Depending on the environment, delivery can include data definitions, integration code, workflow configuration and a shared view of work in progress. The scope must name the systems that will actually be connected and the behavior that will be tested.

The aim is to let a person see what is current, what needs attention and what happened without reconstructing the job from several chats. GR does not offer a proven universal connector catalog. Broader coverage depends on establishing and testing each required connection in the client's environment.

sections.heading: Keep the first release affordable
paragraphs: Choose a complete, useful operation with a limited number of systems and a named owner. Reuse software the company already has where it fits. Separate necessary integration work from optional replacement projects. Include maintenance and exception handling in the estimate, rather than judging cost from a demonstration alone.
Good Remedy scopes implementation after discovery. We do not publish a universal implementation price or claim a demonstrated cost advantage for every environment.

sections.heading: Keep the whole operation in view
paragraphs: A company may want its sales, onboarding, delivery and management work to become connected over time. That is a legitimate buying horizon. Start with one complete function whose result can be used by the next person, while keeping the larger relationships in the design.

The point is not to predict every future workflow. It is to establish where shared meaning and decisions live, how a change affects dependent work, and what each participating tool or person needs to know. The operation should become easier to extend as the business learns.

questions: Can we keep our current AI tools?
Often that is the sensible starting point. Each tool needs to be assessed for the particular job, its access, data handling and ability to exchange the required information.
Do all departments need to change at once?
No. A coherent first operation can cross only the teams and systems needed for its outcome. The wider map helps prevent that first build from becoming another disconnected tool.
What should we bring to a scoping discussion?
A real recurring job, its owner, the tools involved and an example of a handoff or exception that currently requires manual repair.

title: How do you move an AI onboarding pilot into actual operations?
description: Move an AI customer onboarding pilot into daily use with readiness criteria, exception handling, named owners and an accepted handoff into service delivery.
answer: An AI-assisted onboarding operation should carry a customer from an agreed sale to a ready service handoff. That includes collecting information, checking completeness, identifying exceptions, obtaining the required human decisions and passing current commitments to the delivery team. Good Remedy can help scope and build that connected operation around the client's existing systems.

sections.heading: Define what complete means to the receiving team
paragraphs: A customer can be complete in sales and still be unready for service. The commercial terms may be agreed while required documents are missing or an unusual promise has not reached delivery. If an AI labels the account ready from the sales record alone, the next team inherits the unfinished work.

Start with the receiving team’s actual job. What do they need to act, which conditions can remain open, and who may accept an exception? Then work back to the intake. That forms the operation before deciding where extraction, drafting or routing will save effort.

sections.heading: Define what ready means
paragraphs: An uploaded document is not necessarily an accepted document. A completed form does not necessarily mean the customer can enter service. Define the business conditions for readiness before choosing what the AI should automate.

For a service business, readiness could include an agreed scope, named contacts, required documents, an assigned delivery owner and resolved exceptions. The actual conditions depend on the business and remain its responsibility.

sections.heading: Follow the onboarding chain
items: Receive the customer record and commitments made during sales.
Request only the information needed for the agreed service.
Check completeness and identify conflicting or missing information.
Present uncertain cases and consequential decisions to the appropriate person.
Record the decision and hand the accepted information to delivery.
Keep later changes connected to the customer record and affected work.

sections.heading: What people should see
paragraphs: The onboarding coordinator needs a queue showing what is missing and who owns the next step. A reviewer needs the relevant documents and the reason a decision is requested. The delivery owner needs the accepted scope and unresolved conditions. A manager needs to see where customers are waiting and why.

The AI can assist with extraction, comparison, preparation and routing within its access and agreed responsibilities. Permissions in software and the person's authority to accept a customer are separate questions.

sections.heading: Move from demonstration to a supported release
paragraphs: A demonstration may use one clean application and a person who already knows the answer. Daily operation introduces incomplete records, duplicate requests, absent reviewers and changes after approval. List those differences before expanding the pilot.

Run a limited release for one customer type with an owner who can inspect exceptions and pause the automation. Agree how to recover a failed handoff, where to record decisions, and who supports the operation when access or a model changes. Expand after the receiving team can use the result and the observed exceptions have a workable response.

sections.heading: What to test before use
paragraphs: Test a complete application, an incomplete one and a case with contradictory information. Change an accepted field and check whether the right downstream work is reconsidered. Confirm that the receiving person can see what was actually approved.

These are illustrative acceptance checks. A real implementation needs tests for its own systems, data and business requirements. Good Remedy's scope should identify the delivered workflow, integrations, human responsibilities and acceptance evidence.

sections.heading: Improve the work while introducing AI
paragraphs: An onboarding engagement does not have to begin with a broken AI tool. It can begin with an ordinary process that people want to improve. Forming the workflow may reveal duplicate requests, unclear responsibilities or a handoff that depends on one employee’s memory. Fixing those conditions is part of designing a useful AI-enabled operation.

Judge the result by whether the customer reaches service with the right commitments, information and responsible people in place. A faster document summary is one contribution to that outcome. It is not the entire outcome.

questions: Can AI approve onboarding automatically?
Only the agreed operation can determine which actions may be delegated. Consequential decisions need the business's proper authority and any applicable professional requirements.
Is this a replacement for our CRM?
Not necessarily. The CRM may remain the customer record while other tools handle documents, work queues or delivery. The implementation must establish how they stay consistent.
What is a practical starting point?
One customer type and one service with clear intake, readiness and delivery criteria.

title: How do you turn AI sales research into a useful CRM handoff?
description: Help salespeople act on AI research without repeating it: connect account evidence, qualification, contact history and follow-up in a current CRM record.
answer: The research is finished, but the salesperson still has to check the company, reconstruct the reason for contact and work out what to do next. That is the handoff to improve. Carry the evidence, uncertainty, contact history and a reasoned next step into the account record. Good Remedy can help design and implement that chain as part of a connected sales operation.

sections.heading: Transfer the judgment the next person needs
paragraphs: A researcher may understand an account after an hour of reading. Their colleague receives three links and a polished paragraph. What disappeared is why those sources mattered, which possibility was rejected and what would change the proposed approach.

A useful handoff carries enough of that basis for the next person to work independently. It identifies the actual business, the evidence, the remaining hypothesis and the next useful question. It should reduce the need to call the researcher back, while leaving room for the salesperson to disagree with the proposed approach.

sections.heading: Give each signal a disposition
paragraphs: A company announcement, executive change or implementation initiative can justify investigation. It does not establish buying intent on its own. The operation should preserve the signal and its date, identify the company, check duplicates and decide whether to research, monitor, dismiss or route it.
Several signals may belong to the same account. Keeping them together helps a salesperson understand what has changed without treating every mention as a new prospect.

sections.heading: Do the associate-level research
items: Visit the company website and establish what it actually does.
Read the original signal and separate the announcement from assumptions about its meaning.
Identify relevant executives and the person likely to own the work.
Check the company's public contact routes and existing relationship history.
Consult licensed contact tools where available, recording source and verification status.
Look for current news and corroborating information.
Prepare direct business contact details where verified, or preserve the best available front door without guessing.

sections.heading: Deliver a brief someone can act on
paragraphs: The account brief should explain why the company might fit, what remains uncertain, who to approach, what evidence supports the approach and what to ask next. A suggested message should relate to the company's actual situation. The next action needs an owner and a due date.

Contact availability, relationship history and requests not to be contacted belong in the operation. Draft preparation and authorization to send are distinct. Existing CRM and outreach controls should remain connected to the work.

sections.heading: Test the handoff with someone new
paragraphs: Give the brief to a colleague who did not conduct the research. Ask them to identify the current account, the original signal, the proposed contact route and the next action without asking the researcher to reconstruct the work. If they cannot, the handoff needs more than a polished summary.

Preserve source links, dates, the owner and the difference between an observed fact and a proposed approach. When the account changes hands, transfer access to the permitted records and confirm who takes responsibility for open follow-ups. Do not treat a copied chat as evidence that the new owner received the current state.

sections.heading: What happens after a reply
paragraphs: A reply can correct the research, identify another owner, reveal a real project or end the outreach. Preserve that new information in the account record and update the next step. The system should support the salesperson through the conversation rather than continuing a sequence that no longer fits.

This describes a possible implementation scope, not a claim of automated prospecting results. Source access, contact-tool licenses, integrations and sending arrangements must be confirmed for each engagement.

sections.heading: Keep one account current as the conversation develops
paragraphs: Research, a drafted message, a real reply, a meeting and an agreed project are different events. The operation needs to remember which actually occurred. A buyer’s correction should change the account picture and the next action, rather than sit in a separate chat while an old plan keeps running.

If a commercial conversation becomes implementation work, carry the agreed scope and open questions into delivery. Do not make the client explain the same job again because the sales tools and delivery tools belong to different teams.

questions: Does every signal become outreach?
No. Research can support dismissal, monitoring, a request for more evidence or a different contact route. Useful qualification includes deciding when not to proceed.
Can this use Apollo or ZoomInfo?
The operation can be scoped around tools the client is licensed and authorized to use. Actual API access and integration behavior must be checked before promising a connection.
What would the salesperson receive?
A sourced account brief, relevant contact route, reason for the proposed approach, unresolved questions and a named next action.

title: Why do AI workflows break when requirements change?
description: How to investigate repeated context loss, forgotten corrections and broken handoffs in an existing AI workflow, then scope the repair.
answer: A workflow can fail even when the information still exists. The next person or AI worker may recover an older file, miss a settled decision or treat a correction as a fresh proposal. Good Remedy examines what the work depends on and how its accepted state travels between steps. The repair should preserve what is still valid, identify what changed and let the next worker continue from the right place.

sections.heading: The file is there. The work still gets lost.
paragraphs: You finish a discussion, settle a decision and ask for a small amendment. Another chat reviews the result without the same context and reopens the decision. Each response can sound reasonable on its own. Together, they make you carry the agreement between workers and explain why the job is already further along.

This is a general illustration of a problem recorded during GR’s development, not a client case study or proof that one technical remedy solves every instance. It points to a concrete question: does the next worker receive the current work, or merely another document about it?

sections.heading: Start with one real failure
paragraphs: Collect the input, the expected outcome, the returned work and the correction someone had to make. Check whether the worker received an outdated file, a missing decision or instructions for a different stage. A confident answer can still be based on the wrong state of the job.

If people keep pasting the same corrections into new chats, the operation may need a durable way to preserve and supply the accepted state. More context is useful only when the next worker can tell what is current and what authority it carries.

sections.heading: A correction should change what happens next
paragraphs: A correction may fix a fact, change the goal, exercise human authority or challenge the way the whole job has been understood. Those inputs need different treatment. Appending every instruction to a longer prompt does not resolve which earlier assumptions are now wrong.

Record the accepted correction at the level where it belongs. Identify which outputs depended on the old assumption and which can remain. Supply the changed state to the next worker. Then test a new handoff to see whether the correction actually affects the work.

sections.heading: Inspect the whole handoff
items: Where does the accepted decision live?
What tells the next person or AI worker that this is the current version?
Which source or instruction changed?
Which outputs depend on that change?
Who may resolve a disagreement?
How is completed work checked and returned to the system people actually use?

sections.heading: Make the repair observable
paragraphs: An agreed repair might change how context is assembled, how a result is validated, how a human decision is recorded or how the receiving application is updated. The implementation should name the part being changed and preserve a way to compare behavior before and after.

Repeat the original failure case. Then change a source or owner and check the next handoff. Confirm that the operation makes its uncertainty visible and that useful work can continue where the change has no effect.

sections.heading: How Good Remedy can help
paragraphs: Bring the workflow, a recent example and the systems involved. We can help establish what is failing and the scope of a useful repair. A broader redesign may be justified when several disconnected tools share the same unresolved operating problem. The first movement should still have a clear outcome and acceptance criteria.
Implementation is scoped after discovery. This guide does not promise that every context failure has the same cause or that instructions alone can make a model reliable.

sections.heading: Do not make the founder hold the system together
paragraphs: If progress requires someone to remember every decision, choose the right old conversation and keep telling the AI where to resume, that person has become part of the operating infrastructure. Their effort can hide how little continuity the system supplies.

A useful repair should reduce that reconstruction burden. Ask another person to pick up the work, introduce a relevant change, and observe where they still need the original operator. That gives the team a more meaningful test than asking the same well-informed chat whether it remembers.

questions: Should we switch models?
A different model may help some failures. First check whether the current worker had the correct sources, decisions and task. A model change does not resolve a missing business record.
Can we preserve our existing automation?
Yes, where it remains useful. Inspection should distinguish what to retain, adapt, reconnect or replace.
What counts as a successful repair?
The agreed failure is addressed, the required handoff works, and the team has evidence and ownership for continued use.

title: What should AI implementation include besides the model or agent?
description: Questions to ask an AI implementation provider about scope, existing systems, deliverables, ongoing cost, human responsibility and evidence that the operation works.
answer: Choose implementation help by the operation you need delivered. Ask who will define the work, connect the systems, build the software, test exceptions and support the result. Compare providers against the same scope and acceptance criteria. Good Remedy's approach begins with the complete work and an agreed first implementation, including the people and systems that must carry it forward.

sections.heading: Buy the operation your people will use
paragraphs: A model demonstration shows that AI can perform a task. An implementation needs to show how that contribution becomes useful work inside the business. Who brings the request? What does the worker receive? Who decides the unresolved matters? Which system records the result? Who takes it from there?

Walk through the working day of the people involved. The associate needs a usable queue and a way to resolve exceptions. The manager needs current work and decisions that require attention. Leadership needs to understand whether the operation is accomplishing its purpose. The same implementation has to support those related needs.

sections.heading: Different providers can play different parts
paragraphs: A platform specialist may be a strong fit for a defined configuration or integration. An automation firm may build repeatable flows. A broader operating problem may also require someone to establish shared records, human responsibilities and behavior when the work changes.

These roles can be combined. The useful question is whether the engagement covers the operation's needs and whether each responsibility has an owner. This guide is published by Good Remedy, a provider of implementation help. It is our approach to evaluating scope, not an independent vendor ranking.

sections.heading: Ask to see the deliverable
items: Which people will use the delivered software, and what will their working day look like?
Which applications and records will actually be connected?
What can the AI do, and what still requires a person?
What happens when information is missing or contradictory?
What evidence must be produced before the client accepts the work?
Who handles support, model changes, access changes and new exceptions?

sections.heading: Compare the full cost
paragraphs: Separate initial formation and implementation from software licenses, model usage, hosting, support and future changes. Identify work the client's own people must perform. A small subscription may still depend on substantial internal coordination; a larger initial build may include more of that work. Compare actual commitments rather than labels.

For an affordable first engagement, choose a useful operation with bounded integration requirements and reuse existing systems where appropriate. Good Remedy scopes Build and Fix work after discovery. No equivalent-scope cost comparison or universal savings claim is established by this guide.

sections.heading: Start with an operation you can recognize
paragraphs: Examples include moving a customer from intake to service, turning a sales signal into a researched account and follow-up, or keeping delivery work current when scope changes. Each crosses several steps while still having a recognizable outcome.

Ask a prospective provider to walk through a normal case, a difficult exception and a change after launch. That conversation should make the proposed work more concrete. Good Remedy's first conversation starts with the job you want to improve and the tools and people already involved.

sections.heading: Affordability depends on delivery, too
paragraphs: A smaller company can have a complicated operation without an enterprise transformation budget. A practical engagement should reuse what the company already owns, select a complete first function and make later expansion explicit. Reusable delivery machinery can reduce rebuilding across engagements, but the actual hours, support needs and costs still have to be measured.

Ask what you will need to keep doing manually after launch. If the apparent saving depends on a founder continuously repairing the workflow, that work belongs in the cost comparison. Good Remedy’s aim is useful operating capability at a cost proportionate to the job; an equivalent-scope savings claim needs actual delivery evidence.

questions: Do we need a company-wide platform project?
Not necessarily. A complete first operation can be limited in scope while the design accounts for later connections.
How much does Good Remedy implementation cost?
Build and Fix engagements are scoped after discovery. The homepage describes the separately bounded Diligence Readout offer; it is not a general implementation price.
What should we ask before signing?
Ask for specific deliverables, responsibilities, assumptions, acceptance evidence, support arrangements and how changes will be priced and handled.
